Reznor has also achieved recognition as an acclaimed composer for TV and movie soundtracks, earning Oscars, Emmys, and Grammys. "Trent Resner continues to release some of the heaviest material out there, but he's also now in a claim composer of soundtracks for TV and movies. podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails, along with Radiohead, pioneered "grand experiments" in music distribution by leveraging their large fan bases directly. They bypassed traditional record deals and labels, selling products directly to fans and managing their audience without intermediaries. "And then we have the grand experiments by bands such as 9-inch nails and radio head."

podcast.title: Early Label Deal and TVT Dispute
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails' first record deal was with TV Toons, a Chicago label previously specializing in TV theme song compilations, whose president, Steve Gottlieb, rebranded it as TVT. Gottlieb initially expected an "edgier Depeche Mode" but was deeply disappointed by "Pretty Hate Machine," calling it an "abortion" and predicting only 20,000 sales. This led to a "nightmare" legal battle lasting almost two years (1990-1992), during which Trent was contractually prohibited from releasing new music. "However, Trent was beginning to move beyond his favorite techno pop bands and into something a little more sinister and a lot harder."

podcast.title: Early Label Misunderstanding
podcast.body: In 1987, Steve Gottlieb of TVT Records signed Trent Reznor from Cleveland, expecting a Depeche Mode-style band based on his demos. Gottlieb was annoyed when the music turned out to be substantially harder. "TVThead Steve Gottlieb signed this kid from Cleveland named Trent Rezner. Based on the demos he had heard, he thought he was getting a Depeche Mode style band. And he got was actually substantially harder. And he was extremely annoyed."

podcast.title: Financial Struggles During TVT Battle
podcast.body: During the protracted legal dispute with TVT Records, Trent Reznor and Nine Inch Nails faced significant financial challenges due to their restrictive contract. The band's participation in the first Lollapalooza tour in the summer of 1991, where they were paid $12,000 per gig, was crucial. This money largely went towards paying for legal fees, as well as essential living expenses like food and rent, keeping the band afloat during a difficult period. "The $12,000 nine-inch nails was paid for each gig, but a long way towards paying for lawyers, not to mention for things like food and rent."

Bowie's "shape-shifting style" and introduction of "more theater, fantasy, and imagination" into rock and roll culture provided foundational inspiration for bands like Nine Inch Nails. podcast.title: Kraftwerk Influence
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails, a key band in industrial music, is mentioned as being influenced by Kraftwerk. "Industrial music starting in the late 70s and going through 9-inch nails and beyond. Craftwork."

podcast.title: Legal Defense by Charles B. Ortoner
podcast.body: Trent Reznor was defended in his plagiarism lawsuit by Charles B. Ortoner, a New York-based lawyer specializing in such cases. podcast.title: Mercer, Pennsylvania Origins - Population 2,391
podcast.body: The roots of Nine Inch Nails are found in Mercer, Pennsylvania, a town with a population of 2,391. It is located about an hour north of Pittsburgh and 90 minutes east of Cleveland. "The roots of nine-inch nails are found in Mercer, Pennsylvania, which is about an hour north of Pittsburgh and about 90 minutes east of Cleveland. Population 2391."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Move to Cleveland for Music
podcast.body: Music eventually led Trent Reznor to the big city of Cleveland, where he secured jobs at a music store and then a recording studio, setting the stage for the Nine Inch Nails story. "But music kept drawing his attention away to the big city of Cleveland. He moved there, got a job at a music store, then a recording studio, and then, you know, the nine-inch nail story after that, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Reflecting Synthesizer Evolution (1990s)
podcast.body: A track by Nine Inch Nails is played as a "contribute to Hugh Lacane, the inventor of the earliest form of keyboard synthesizer." This implies that the band's work, particularly Trent Reznor's contributions in the 1990s, exemplifies the lineage and impact of electronic keyboard synthesizers that Le Caine pioneered decades earlier. "A little 9 inch nails, contribute to Hugh Lacane, the inventor of the earliest form of keyboard synthesizer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nine-Inch Diameter Record
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails once released a record that was precisely 9 inches in diameter, a deliberate choice that played on the band's name and offered a unique physical format. "9 inch nails. Once released a record, 9 inches in diameter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ninja Tour Co-Headliner
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails co-headlined the "Ninja tour" with Jane's Addiction, a tour named after the initials NIN and JA. "That was a great name for a tour, NIN, Nine Inch Nails and J.A. Jane's addiction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nothing Records – Vanity Boutique Label
podcast.body: Trent Reznor's Nothing Records was created by Interscope, a subsidiary of Universal, as a special vanity boutique label. This arrangement gave Trent Reznor extra creative control, allowing him to pursue, sign, develop, and produce talent independently. It exemplifies how major labels can establish indie-looking imprints for significant artists. "This gave Trent some extra creative control and allowed him to pursue, sign, develop and produce talent on his own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opening Act for Peter Murphy
podcast.body: A "little band out of Cleveland called Nine-inch Nails" served as the opening act for Peter Murphy during his tour to promote his "Deep" album, introducing them to thousands of new listeners. "Little band out of Cleveland called Nine-inch Nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus

podcast.title: Origin of the Name "Nine Inch Nails"
podcast.body: The name "Nine Inch Nails" does not carry any special meaning or symbolism, despite potential rumors. Trent Reznor simply came up with it while doodling names and liked how it sounded, so he decided to keep it. "Well, nowhere really. It doesn't mean anything special, despite any rumors that you may have heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Personal Struggles and Grandmother's Death (Mid-Late 1990s)
podcast.body: Trent Reznor suffered from depression and a social anxiety disorder. The death of his grandmother, who raised him, profoundly affected him, leading to heavy drinking, cocaine use, and ultimately heroin addiction by the late 1990s. His association with Marilyn Manson during this period was also noted as unhelpful. "The death of his grandmother, the woman who raised him really messed him up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Piano as the Foundational Compositional Instrument
podcast.body: A significant portion of Nine Inch Nails' tracks originate as piano compositions, directly stemming from Trent Reznor's classical training. The piano serves as the fundamental basis for the band's unique sound and overall artistic direction, providing a core structure to their complex arrangements. "A big chunk of nine-inch nails tracks start as piano compositions because of his classical training. He's just more comfortable sitting at a piano than anywhere else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Popularity of Industrial Music (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails was cited as a prominent group driving the popularity of Industrial music in the early and mid-1990s. "Industrial music was hot thanks to groups like Nine Inge Nails and Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Cure Influence
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails was also cited as a group influenced by The Cure, highlighting the diverse impact of The Cure's music on subsequent artists, despite Nine Inch Nails' primary genre being industrial. "if you're looking for bands influenced by them we can turn to groups like Interpol, Smashing Pumpkins, The Killers, Nine-H Nails, My Chemical Romance, and so many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-High School Education and Wilderness Living
podcast.body: After graduating high school, Trent Reznor enrolled in a computer course at a nearby college in Meadville (population 15,000). However, he dropped out and spent about a year living in the woods with his father before music drew his attention to Cleveland. "The train graduated from high school. He enrolled in a computer course at nearby college in Medville, which had a population of 15,000. But he dropped out and went to live in the woods with his father for about a year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Production by Alan Moulder
podcast.body: Alan Moulder worked in production with Nine Inch Nails, demonstrating his versatility and rock background. "había trabajado en proceso de producción con Nine Hiss Nails"

podcast.title: Record Label Disinterest in Tapeworm
podcast.body: The record labels for both Nine Inch Nails and Maynard James Keenan were reportedly "not keen" on the Tapeworm project. This lack of label support, along with scheduling conflicts and internal band dynamics, ultimately prevented the album from being released, despite recording sessions in New Orleans and Atlanta in 2003. "But then reality set in. 9 inch nails record label and Maynard's labels weren't keen on the idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Record Sales
podcast.body: The band has sold at least 20 million records. "At least 20 million records have been sold."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Red Horse Virus and Cleveland Massacre Link
podcast.body: Playing "The Great Destroyer" in mono audio unexpectedly revealed the phrase "Red Horse Vector," which led to the website RedHorseVector.net. This site served as a narrative device, explaining that a fictional Red Horse virus was responsible for a "mass psychosis" that culminated in the Cleveland nightclub massacre, thereby connecting disparate clues within the ARG.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab and Detox (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: After his overdose in London, Trent Reznor eventually decided to confront his addictions. He checked into a rehab facility in New Orleans and underwent a severe detox. "He checked into a rehab facility in New Orleans and went through a severe detox."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Remastering of "Pretty Hate Machine"
podcast.body: Trent Reznor wished to remaster "Pretty Hate Machine" for the 21st century as 1989 studio technology was not as advanced as 2010. Legal disputes meant the original masters were inaccessible, causing the album to be out of print for years. In March 2010, The Bicycle Music Company acquired the rights and allowed Reznor to remaster it. The remastered version featured more forward vocals, greater clarity in arrangements, brighter piano, and reduced hiss. "But that changed in March of 2010 when the rights to the master recording were acquired by a company called the Bicycle Music Company. They allowed Trent access to these masters so he could remaster them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Remixing Songs with Hidden Clues
podcast.body: On April 26, 2007, the songs "Capital G," "My Violent Hearts," and "Me I'm Not" were released in GarageBand format for Mac computers. This initiative explicitly encouraged fan remixes, but more importantly, their multi-tracks were embedded with additional hidden clues for the "Year Zero" ARG, prominently linked to the phrase "Google Exhibit 24."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return of Bigger Older Acts Post 9/11
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails was among the established acts whose popularity saw a return after 9/11 and the subsequent wars, as the public mood shifted away from happy music and rock began to experience a resurgence. "And a return of some bigger older acts, U2, 9-H nails, Green Day, Weezer."

podcast.title: Returning the Favor to Jane's Addiction
podcast.body: Trent Reznor later "returned the favor" to Jane's Addiction by getting involved in their reunion, recording songs with them, and touring together in the summer of 2009. "And it was a good pairing too because that first law of Paloza tour saved Trent Resner from financial ruin in 1991. He was just kind of returning the favor."

podcast.title: Sampling of Funky Drummer Break
podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails is listed among the diverse artists who have sampled Clyde Stubblefield's drum break from James Brown's "Funky Drummer." "But also Ed Sheeran, Britney Spears, Nine Inch Nails, Kenny G, Stone Roses, Poppullet itself, and Shanato Conner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sampling on Pretty Hate Machine
podcast.body: The debut album "Pretty Hate Machine" extensively utilized samples from various artists, including Jane's Addiction, Public Enemy, and This Mortal Coil. These samples were often heavily modified and mutilated by computers, making them largely unrecognizable in the final tracks, a technique Chris Vrenna was particularly skilled at. "For example, if you go through that first album, you'll hear samples from Jane's Addiction, Public Enemy, This Mortal Coil, and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Self-Medication and Superstardom
podcast.body: Reznor admitted that in the mid-90s, when he achieved superstardom, he was "ill-equipped to deal with that" and began self-medicating. This initially made him feel "more interesting" and able to navigate social situations, but he "had no idea what I was up against." "I think in the mid-90s, when superstardom set in and I was ill-equipped to deal with that to begin with, I started relying on self-medicating to get through those things and that made me more interesting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Small Town Perspective on Life and Music
podcast.body: Trent Reznor articulated his experience growing up in small-town America, noting a limited scope of travel and the uniformity of amenities like Kmarts and movie theaters showing the same five Sylvester Stallone films. He felt playing music wasn't considered "cool" and that being in the band rather than the football team made you a "leper." "My scope of travel was maybe a half hour radius, and every town had the same Kmart and synoplex, all playing the same five movies, all Sylvester Stallone. It's hard for people who grow up in cities to understand that, to have an endless cornfield in your backyard. But that's what a lot of America is. It's not dodging gunfire from gangs. It wasn't cool to play music where I was, and I got a pretty bad education because I had a bad attitude. If I wanted to get good grades, I could. Stuff I'd like to know now, at the time, I thought was irrelevant. Typical teenage stupidity. I hated school. The fact that it revolved around something you didn't have access to. If you weren't on the football team and you were in the band, you were a leper. When people say those are the best years of our lives, I want to scream. But my parents allowed me to do things that my friends weren't allowed to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Songwriting Philosophy
podcast.body: Trent Reznor's songwriting for "Pretty Hate Machine" and subsequent works was deeply rooted in honest, personal experience. Lacking a guitar-centric background, he utilized computers to simulate sounds, allowing him a broad sonic palette. He focused on relating his own feelings and dissatisfactions with relationships, religion, or government, disguising them to avoid preaching, aiming for relatability rather than political commentary. "So the only thing I could speak about with any authority was my own personal experience and tried to relate situations I'd been into or feelings I'd thought, or dissatisfactions with relationships or religion or the government of the country I live in, or whatever it is."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Successor of No Wave Philosophy
podcast.body: Industrial rock bands like Nine Inch Nails are difficult to understand without exploring the No Wave movement, which significantly shaped their sound and philosophical approach to music. "Incluso otros movimientos de roc muy posteriores, pues como podía ser tú, como podía ser el roc industrial de Nine Is Neys o Grim Theater, incluso bandas eclecticas como Prima de stream, yo creo que son muy difíciles entender sin adentrarse en el no wave."

podcast.title: Surprise Los Angeles Show (The Raid)
podcast.body: On April 18, 2007, the day after "Year Zero" was released, a surprise Nine Inch Nails show took place in Los Angeles. Fans who had successfully cracked codes throughout the ARG were given cell phones and then transported on blacked-out buses to an old warehouse. There, they navigated a maze patrolled by armed guards (actors) and were addressed by a figure claiming to be the leader of the Open Source Resistance before the four-song performance began. The concert dramatically concluded with a staged raid by a fake SWAT team, featuring flash grenades, smoke, and screaming, serving as a "semi finale" to the entire game.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Survivalism Video Clues
podcast.body: The music video for "Survivalism," distributed via pin drives at a London concert, contained hidden time codes. Fans meticulously deciphered these codes to uncover additional websites, highlighting the layered and interactive nature of the ARG's clues.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Synth Pop's Continued Presence in the 90s
podcast.body: While 80s-style Technopop declined in the 1990s, elements of synth pop continued to live on and be present in their music. "It did, however, live in some respects in the music of nine-inch nails, de Pesh mode, radio head, and Bjork."

podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails, fronted by Trent Reznor, is noted for regularly engaging in the destruction of their stage equipment during performances. "Trent Rezner and Nine-inch nails? Seeing them wreck their stuff many times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: T-Shirt Clue Discovery in Lisbon
podcast.body: On February 7, 2007, during the opening night of Nine Inch Nails' European tour in Lisbon, Portugal, local photographer Nuno Foros noticed bolded, seemingly random letters on the back of tour t-shirts. These letters, when deciphered, spelled out "iamtryingtobelieve.com," marking the official beginning of the "Year Zero" Alternate Reality Game.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: T-Shirt Phone Number Clue
podcast.body: A week after the Lisbon concert, on February 14, 2007, a fan named Sue discovered bolded numbers on her Nine Inch Nails t-shirt. These numbers formed a phone number for Los Angeles, which, when dialed, played a recorded message featuring a brief presidential address accompanied by background music. This discovery rapidly disseminated among fans worldwide.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: TVT's Role in Success
podcast.body: Despite the label's initial annoyance, Nine Inch Nails' songs would not have been released without TVT Records, highlighting the indie label's crucial role in the band's early career. "Still, without TVT, we would have never gotten songs like this. Nine-Inch Stales from the days they were in Indie Band recording for Chicago's TVT records."

podcast.title: The Presence Image
podcast.body: A distinctive, alien-looking hand reaching downwards was revealed through a spectral analysis of the audio file for the song "My Violent Hearts." Fans quickly adopted the moniker "The Presence" for this mysterious image.

podcast.title: Toured with The Dresden Dolls
podcast.body: The Dresden Dolls were considered "Goth enough" to be invited on tour with Nine Inch Nails. "Goth enough to be invited on tour with Nine-Hitch Nails"

podcast.title: Touring Partners
podcast.body: Explosions in the Sky, a Texas-based post-rock band, toured with Nine Inch Nails. "They've toured with nine-inch nails, Fugazi, and here's that name again, Godspeed, New Black Emperor."

podcast.title: Transition to Interscope Records
podcast.body: The band was eventually rescued from its legal quagmire with TVT Records by Interscope. Trent Reznor initially viewed this move as "the lesser of several evils" at the time, initially wary due to his perception of Interscope's then-image (associated with Marky Mark). However, he later expressed happiness with the situation, appreciating Interscope's label president who was also a producer, understanding the creative process and potential difficulties artists face. "They rescued us from TBT, it was a lesser of several evils, and at the time my vision of the inner scope was Mark E. Mark, it was like, Christ, one TVT, and another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Trent Resner's Embrace of Remixes
podcast.body: Trent Resner, the driving force behind Nine Inch Nails, exhibited a profound appreciation for the possibilities of the remix, frequently releasing full albums and EPs dedicated solely to remixed Nine Inch Nails material. His enthusiasm extended to performing remix "surgery" on songs by other artists. "Trent Resner loves the possibilities of the remix. In fact he was so into it that he released albums and EPs full of remix 9-inch nails material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor as a Diehard Bowie Fan
podcast.body: Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails was, and remains, a diehard fan of David Bowie. This admiration led to collaborations, including touring together and Reznor appearing in the creepy stalker video for Bowie's 1997 song "I'm Afraid of Americans," which Reznor also remixed. "Brian Rezner was and always will be a diehard Bowie fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Addiction and Recovery
podcast.body: After the last tour in 2001, Trent Reznor recognized he was at a breaking point due to alcoholism and addiction, which had consumed and destroyed him. Faced with a choice between death and recovery, he sought help and committed to turning his life around, realizing he wasn't ready to die. He began to focus on self-care, acknowledging his past reliance on self-medication to cope with early superstardom in the mid-90s. He had initially tried to address his addiction secretly in 1997 while recording 'The Fragile', believing he was cured upon its release, only to experience a severe relapse that lasted a year and a half and nearly cost him his life. His recovery journey involved learning humility, acknowledging his limitations, and taking time off to heal and reconnect with himself, all while fearing he might have lost his ability to write sober. "My soul had been crushed by being an alcoholic and an addict. And there was no denying at that point. And it had consumed me and destroyed me. And there was a fork in the road and it was either death by my own hand or from any number of other ways it could have happened or fix myself."

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Band
podcast.body: Trent Reznor, a major fan of Godspeed You! Black Emperor, is associated with Nine Inch Nails. "And Trent Resner of Nine-East Nails is a major fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Disgust with Contemporary Music
podcast.body: Following his recovery, Trent Reznor expressed strong dissatisfaction with the music scene of the early 2000s, criticizing what he perceived as formulaic sounds and bands that merely emulated older groups. He felt this trend lacked originality and exploited a younger audience's unfamiliarity with the original artists who created the foundational sounds and aesthetics. "Generally, I've been pretty disgusted with music in the last several years. The sound like formula and the new trend of emulating a cool old band is somehow a legitimate reason to have a career today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Grandfather's Company
podcast.body: Trent Reznor's grandfather funded an HVAC company decades ago named "Resner," which is the name seen on large industrial heaters in warehouses. "That's the name of the H. Vat company funded by his grandfather decades and decades ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Lyrics Philosophy
podcast.body: Trent Reznor, the frontman for Nine Inch Nails, initially expressed a reluctance to print lyrics in liner notes. He preferred that listeners engage deeply with the music itself, rather than reading along, though he eventually softened this stance. "Trent Resner of Nine-Hitch Nails wasn't crazy about printing his lyrics, thinking that he'd rather have people listen carefully to the music than follow along."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Rehab and Recovery
podcast.body: After the Tapeworm project faced challenges, Trent Reznor entered rehab. Upon his recovery, he expressed a desire to refocus on Nine Inch Nails, a decision that further impacted the viability and completion of the Tapeworm album, especially given Maynard James Keenan's commitments to other bands. "Meanwhile, Trent went into rehab. And when he recovered, he wanted to get back into 9 inch nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Upbringing
podcast.body: Trent Reznor was raised by his grandparents after his parents divorced. He described Mercer as a "pretty conservative place." "Trent was brought up by his grandparents after his parents divorced. The town is a pretty conservative place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: US Wiretap and Bureau of Morality
podcast.body: The fictional company responsible for the Cleveland wiretap message was named US Wiretap. Its website identified it as a "partnership corporation of the Bureau of Morality." This fictional bureau claimed its agents had intentionally bolted the doors of the Cleveland nightclub because it was a "hangout for the resistance," leading to 112 deaths, which they justified as being "for the good of the nation" within the future timeline.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: USB Key "Leaks"
podcast.body: As part of the ARG, USB keys containing new songs were deliberately "lost" in bathrooms at various European tour venues. The first instance involved a fan named Anna finding a key in Lisbon with "My Violent Hearts," and another key was found simultaneously in the men's bathroom. Later, on February 19, 2007, a key found in Barcelona contained "Me I'm Not," and another found in Manchester, England, on February 25, 2007, held "In This Twilight" along with an image of the destroyed Hollywood sign.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Video Game Music (Quake, Doom 3, Call of Duty)
podcast.body: Trent Reznor created original music for the game "Quake" in 1996, which included Nine Inch Nails Easter eggs. He was slated to work on "Doom 3" but never completed the project. In 2012, he composed the theme music for "Call of Duty 3, Black Ops 2." "In 1996, he created some original music for the game Quake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Nine Inch Nails gigs were among those that featured vigorous mosh pits in the 1990s, demonstrating the widespread adoption of moshing as a tribal behavior in the alternative rock scene. xref.body: Tapeworm was conceived as a side project during Nine Inch Nails' "The Downward Spiral" sessions in 1994, intended as a collaborative effort for Danny Lohner and Charlie Clouser. It evolved to include a star-studded lineup: Trent Reznor, Maynard James Keenan (Tool), producer Alan Molder, Atticus Ross, Phil Anselmo and Rex Brown (Pantera), Page Hamilton (Helmet), Toni Halliday (Curve), Tommy Victor (Ministry), and drummer Josh Freese, with at least an album's worth of material recorded by 2001. "If you're Trent Rezner, Danny Loaner and Charlie Closer from his live band, Maynard James Keenan from Tool, producer Alan Molder and Atticus Ross. I mean, wow, awesome, right? The idea for tapeworm went as far back as the sessions for the downward spiral in 1994. Tapeworm was designed as something to which Danny and Charlie could contribute as equals. This idea evolved into something pretty cool. Maynard was brought in, Phil and Salmo from Pantera, Paige Hamilton from Helmut, Tony Haliday from a cool band called Curve, Tommy Victor from Ministry, drummer Josh Freeze. xref.body: Trent Reznor holds the record for the most weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart due to his songwriting credit on Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road." xref.title: Early Career and Studio Work
xref.body: Trent initially considered a job making synthesizers but instead moved to Cleveland, working in a music store that sold many keyboards. This allowed him to experiment with the latest gear. Later, in late 1987 or early 1988, he found work at The Right Track recording studio in Cleveland, performing menial tasks like gathering cables and cleaning toilets. During the quiet hours, usually between 3 and 8 AM, he had the studio to himself to develop what would become the first Nine Inch Nails album. "By this time, late 87 early 1988, Trent had found work in Cleveland in a recording studio called The Right Track."

xref.title: Financial Struggles During TVT Battle
xref.body: During the protracted legal dispute with TVT Records, Trent Reznor and Nine Inch Nails faced significant financial challenges due to their restrictive contract. The band's participation in the first Lollapalooza tour in the summer of 1991, where they were paid $12,000 per gig, was crucial. This money largely went towards paying for legal fees, as well as essential living expenses like food and rent, keeping the band afloat during a difficult period. "The $12,000 nine-inch nails was paid for each gig, but a long way towards paying for lawyers, not to mention for things like food and rent."

xref.title: Frustration and Evolution with "Broken"
xref.body: While battling TVT Records, Trent felt immense frustration, amplified by the unexpected success of Nine Inch Nails, which made him uncomfortable. Facing the prospect of being unable to release new music due to the legal dispute, and dealing with personal crises, he channeled these feelings into the "Broken" EP. He aimed for a more aggressive sound, experimenting with real guitars and drums, having previously only used machine buttons. He also harbored a desire to "commercially destroy" Nine Inch Nails with this record. "I also was faced with the prospect of it all being over because I couldn't put in music anymore because of this f***ing record label that I was on, and I was on some personal crises at the same time, so it all got focused into that little EP of hate."
